1.pericope_label: One found slain in the field, and the elders and judges measure to the cities round about

schools.summary: Gill places the law after the laws of war as a case of private violence and reports without deciding the dispute over whether the elders and judges are local or come from the great council at Jerusalem; Calvin grounds the whole rite in the preciousness of human life and argues that leaving murder unpunished implicates a community in the guilt.

Henry contrasts this case with the wilful murderer already provided for and warns that the land is not safe from pollution merely because the failure to punish was nobody’s fault, granting that providence often brings such deeds to light but not always, so that secrecy is made good only for a while.

Keil identifies the elders as representatives of the communities and the judges as administrators of right, explains that what is measured is the distance from the body to each surrounding town, and gives two reasons why the nearest bears the expiation, the direction of suspicion and the burden of the guilt itself.

Wesley explains that the field is named only because such murders most commonly happen there, reads the phrase as a single class of elders who are judges, and notes that measuring was superfluous where the nearest city was already evident.

debates: Who goes out to measure: Aben Ezra and Wesley keep it local, the elder-judges of the neighbouring cities, while the Targum and the rabbinic rulings Gill cites send a delegation from the great council at Jerusalem and argue over its size.
outliers: Calvin turns the law forward into an argument against impunity, reasoning that if an undiscoverable murder still defiles a community, a discoverable one left unpunished defiles it far worse.

3.pericope_label: The elders take an unyoked heifer down to a rough valley and break its neck

schools.summary: Calvin explains the unyoked animal as making satisfaction by innocent blood the more vivid and the desert place as carrying the pollution away from cultivated ground; Gill reads the valley as an emblem of the low estate into which Christ came.

Henry denies outright that the heifer was a sacrifice, since it was never brought to the altar, calling it a solemn protestation of what they would have done to the murderer had they held him, and passes on the tradition that the valley was never afterwards tilled or sown unless the murderer was found.

Clarke reads the Hebrew for the place as possibly a rapid stream through uncultivated ground, treats the rite as a sacrifice of atonement which would therefore pollute tilled land, and notes that the law was framed to keep murder in abhorrence and magistrates alert so that offenders might be found and public expense saved; Wesley reads the desert place as begetting horror of murder and the unyoked heifer both as the murderer who would not bear God’s yoke and as a type of Christ, who bore one voluntarily.
Keil specifies an animal never worked and never yoked, whose vital force had not been diminished by labour, brought down to a valley of constantly flowing water and killed by breaking the neck.

debates: Whether the heifer was a sacrifice: Clarke calls it a sacrifice made to atone for the murder and explains the untilled ground by that, Henry denies it was a sacrifice at all since it never came to the altar, and Calvin allows that it represented satisfaction by innocent blood while stopping short of calling it a price paid to God.
outliers: Wesley makes the same animal stand for two opposite figures at once, the murderer who refused the yoke of the law and the Christ who took a yoke upon himself.

5.pericope_label: The priests come near, and the elders wash their hands over the heifer

schools.summary: Gill notes that the sons of Levi marks men whose descent was beyond question, and places these at the court in Jerusalem to direct the rite and settle difficulties; Calvin explains the washing as a check against protesting inconsiderately, since it was as though they had set the corpse before God and stood opposite it to purge away the crime.

Henry infers from the priests trying every controversy that God being Israel’s King his ministers must be their magistrates, presses that the elders swore to more than a bare denial, and judges that Pilate wretchedly misapplied the rite if he had it in view, since protestations are worth nothing against the fact.

Clarke identifies the hand-washing as an ancient sign of innocence and conjectures that Pilate learned it from the Jews; Wesley extends every controversy beyond a mortal stroke to any wound one man gives another.

Keil limits the priests to attending witnesses who receive the declaration and authorise the act rather than conducting it, and reads the hand-washing as a symbolic clearing of the town from any suspicion of part in the murder.

debates: What Pilate was doing: Clarke reads his hand-washing as the same rite borrowed from Jewish practice, while Henry allows the allusion only to condemn it, since a protestation is worth nothing against the sentence he had just passed.
outliers: Henry alone spells out how far the oath reached, covering not only the shedding of blood but any concealment of the murderer or help in his escape.

7.pericope_label: Our hands have not shed this blood: the prayer, and the blood forgiven

schools.summary: Gill records that the prayer is assigned by some to the elders continuing their declaration and by the Targums and rabbinic sources to the priests; Calvin gives two motives for it, their own possible carelessness and the fear that vengeance might spread as it once did through the sacrilege of one man, and denies that the heifer was a price of satisfaction, grounding forgiveness in humble reconciliation and the shutting of the door against future murders.

Henry assumes the priests speak, explains that the murderer might well be of that city or harboured in it so that they must ask not to fare the worse for him, and turns the petition outward into a duty of interceding for a guilty land, emptying by prayer the measure that others fill by their sins.

Keil follows the case past its close, noting that the death inflicted vicariously on the animal was a substitute only for an absent criminal, so that a murderer discovered afterwards would still suffer it himself.
Wesley distinguishes the two kinds of guilt at issue, no mortal guilt in the people but a ceremonial uncleanness in the land, and it is that which had to be expiated and forgiven.

debates: Who speaks the prayer: the words read as the elders continuing, but Gill reports the Targums and the rabbinic tradition assigning them to the priests, and Henry writes as though the priests were the speakers throughout.
outliers: Keil alone follows the case past its close, noting that the heifer’s death would not shield a murderer later found.

10.pericope_label: A beautiful woman among the captives, desired for a wife

schools.summary: Gill restricts the law to a war of Israel’s own choosing, since the wars God commanded left no captives, and reports the rabbinic view that the woman might be virgin, wife or widow; Calvin reads the law as parallel to the rules on food, judges that abstaining altogether would have been better, observes how much licence conquerors allow themselves, and says God tempers his indulgence so that men in the fervour of lust retain some religious affection.

Henry calls the permission an indulgence granted for hardness of heart, given lest men denied it defile themselves and trouble the camp, and measures it against the gospel on three counts before concluding that here the law of Christ far exceeds in glory the law of Moses.

Clarke insists that no forcible possession was allowed even here, where ancient usage counted the woman part of the spoil, and that the man might not use her in any inferior character; Wesley suggests the phrase about desire may cover more than intention and reads the passage as treating two cases, the captor who marries her and the one who does not.
Keil argues from the opening formula that the law concerns wars with surrounding nations after the conquest and not the Canaanites who were to be cut off.

debates: What kind of concession this is: Henry calls it an indulgence to hardness of heart and openly ranks the gospel above it, while Calvin, reaching much the same verdict on the conduct, presents the law as God restraining a licence conquerors would otherwise take entirely unchecked.
outliers: Clarke alone reads the law chiefly as a protection, stressing what the captor was forbidden rather than what he was permitted.

12.pericope_label: Her head shaven, a month of mourning, and her release if he has no delight in her

schools.summary: Gill preserves a rabbinic rationale opposite to the others, that her finery was taken away to abate her captor’s ardour, and takes the raiment of captivity for the fine garments she was captured in; Calvin detaches the release from the marriage law, assigning it to the commandment against defrauding rather than that against adultery, and weighs liberty against chastity in reckoning what the woman is left with.

Clarke makes the shaving a renunciation of her old religion and her reception as a proselyte, notes the custom surviving in the East, and doubts the usual rendering of the nails, suspecting the staining of them with henna rather than paring or growing; Wesley agrees on the shaving, reads the raiment of captivity as the sordid clothes put on her when taken, and spells out that making merchandise of her covers both servile work and prostitution.

Keil takes the shaving and the cutting of the nails as customary signs of purification, symbols of her passing out of slavery into the fellowship of the covenant nation, and explains the month as time to console herself for the loss of her parents so that she might give herself henceforth to her husband.

debates: Why her head is shaved: Keil makes it purification and adoption into the covenant people, Clarke and Wesley make it renunciation of heathen religion, and Gill preserves a rabbinic explanation that it was meant to cool the desire of the man who wanted her.

What the raiment of her captivity is: Gill takes it for the finery she was captured in and had to exchange for worn clothes, while Wesley and Keil take it for the prisoner’s clothing she had been put into.
outliers: Calvin alone reclassifies the release under a different commandment, treating it as a question of property and restitution rather than of chastity, so that the penalty of lust is the loss of the booty.

15.pericope_label: If a man have two wives, one beloved and another hated

schools.summary: Gill treats two wives as supposed but not approved, permitted for hardness of heart against the order of creation, the law being made only to prevent confusion once the custom had taken hold.

Henry reads the verse as an exhibit against having more than one wife, listing the strife, jealousy and vexation it must produce, and suggests the law left it unrestrained in hope that experience of its inconvenience would end it; he also finds in the framing of the case a rule of providence, that God sides with the weakest and gives more abundant honour to the part that lacked.

Clarke establishes that hated means loved less throughout Scripture, illustrating from Jacob and Leah and from Jacob loved and Esau hated, and holds that Moses suffered polygamy under regulation without ever enjoining it; Wesley states that the practice is tolerated rather than made lawful and that the law provides only for the children.

outliers: Henry alone turns the case into a providential rule rather than a legal one, reading the mother of the firstborn as compensated for being the less loved wife.

16.pericope_label: He shall acknowledge the son of the hated for the firstborn, giving him a double portion

schools.summary: Calvin classifies the law as a part and supplement of the commandment against stealing, since substituting one son for another is a kind of theft, explains why polygamy in particular made the safeguard necessary, calls the reassignment of a birthright a near claim to the power of creating, and yet allows a substitution where there is just cause; Gill describes the mechanics, the division by will, word of mouth or deed of gift, and the acknowledgment that separates the firstborn and makes him known to all.
Keil states the substance of the right, a double portion of everything the father has, on the ground that this son is the beginning of his strength.

debates: Whether a firstborn may ever be passed over: the prohibition reads flatly, but Calvin allows that where there is just cause for disinheriting him another may be substituted, and cites Jacob for it.
outliers: Calvin grounds the law in a psychological claim the text does not make, that a man who takes a second wife thereby shows he never truly loved the first.

18.pericope_label: A stubborn and rebellious son, brought by both his parents to the elders

schools.summary: Gill reports a rabbinic reason for the sequence, that captive marriages often produced refractory children, describes the offender as stubborn in nature and rebellious in action, and records the rule that neither parent acting alone makes a son liable; Calvin generalises the law to all who insult father or mother, derives from it what honouring them means, and praises the procedure as a moderation of the severity, setting it against a Roman father’s private power of life and death.

Henry takes the order of the two laws as deliberate, since impartiality requires that children owe their parents what parents owe their children, and excludes weakness of capacity from the charge, confining it to wilfulness before listing the conduct meant.

Clarke calls the law a powerful preventive of crime and wishes it in force and duly executed today; Wesley explains the requirement of both parents as a guard against cruelty, judges the law righteous once such consent is given, and treats the bringing of the son to the elders as a second caution against hard-hearted parents.
Keil states the double aim of these laws, that they defend parental authority and at the same time limit it.

outliers: Clarke alone treats the law as a live proposal rather than an antiquity, regretting that no such statute is enforced now.

20.pericope_label: This our son is stubborn and rebellious: the men of his city shall stone him

schools.summary: Gill records the Targum that has the parents confess their own sin before accusing, describes a graduated procedure of admonition and beating before three judges prior to any stoning, preserves a tradition allowing the son to be spared on repentance, and reports that the Jews held the law never to have been executed; Calvin argues that a trial must be inferred, since judges who pronounced nothing would be sitting like ciphers, lists the abuses a hearing was meant to catch, and reads the closing clause as purging the land and making an example.

Keil takes gluttony and drunkenness as the explanation of the son’s refractoriness, and holds that no evidence or judicial inquiry is contemplated at all, the elders not being judges in the strict sense, since the willingness of parents to give up their own child was itself the proof; what the law does is transfer the power of execution from the parents to the town while leaving their authority intact.
Wesley reads the two named vices as standing for others of like or worse nature, and states that the elders were first to examine the cause with all exactness and only then pronounce sentence.

debates: Whether the son was tried: Keil holds that no inquiry is contemplated and the parents’ charge was proof in itself, while Calvin infers a full hearing from the presence of judges and insists the son must have been allowed to plead, listing the parental malice, stepmother’s instigation and fits of passion such a hearing would expose; Wesley and Gill both describe examination and a graduated procedure.
outliers: Gill alone reports that the law was held never to have been carried out, which puts the whole dispute over its procedure at one remove from practice.

22.pericope_label: If a man have committed a sin worthy of death, and thou hang him on a tree

schools.summary: Gill takes the opening clause as covering any capital offence and reports the rabbinic restriction of it to the recognised modes of execution; Calvin explains the precept as aimed at the living, to banish barbarism and impress a horror of even a just execution, grounds the rights of burial in the resurrection and in sparing the eyes of the living, insists that God sanctions the mode of punishment while abhorring atrocity, and denies that accursed passes any verdict on the man’s salvation.

Keil holds that the hanging is not the means of execution but a further exposure of a man already put to death with the sword, an intensification of the penalty, and glosses the phrase for a capital offence as literally a right of death.
Wesley agrees that the hanging followed a death inflicted some other way, the public shame being added to the punishment already suffered.

outliers: Calvin alone distinguishes between God sanctioning a mode of execution and God abominating what is done with the body afterwards, so that the same law both permits the gallows and forbids leaving a man on it.

23.pericope_label: His body shall not remain all night upon the tree, for he that is hanged is accursed of God

schools.summary: Gill applies the rule to everyone hanged, fixes the removal at sunset from the Targum and the rabbis, and extends the principle to any unburied body kept overnight unless it is kept for its own honour; Calvin allows the phrase real force as a mark of God’s curse while denying that it despairs of the man’s salvation, and names Paul as the one who applies the passage to Christ.

Henry takes accursed of God to signify no more than the highest disgrace and reproach, a man hanging between heaven and earth being reckoned abandoned by both, and holds that the Spirit chose the phrase in this weaker sense precisely so that it might afterwards be applied to the death of Christ.

Clarke reads the single day of exposure as measured to serve public justice without a permanent exhibition of a decaying body, turns the verse against the spiking of heads and the gibbeting of criminals in his own day as barbarism that never prevented the crimes it punished, explains the curse as a forfeiture to the law alighting on the body, and finds mercy walking hand in hand with judgment in the Mosaic penalties; Wesley reads the curse at its strongest, as a singular punishment by God’s appointment which is therefore sufficient without the added shame of lying unburied.
Keil gives the clause and its reason without expounding either, letting the prohibition and the defilement of the land stand as written.

debates: What accursed of God means: Henry reduces it to extreme disgrace and reproach, Wesley raises it to a singular punishment inflicted by God’s own appointment, Clarke makes it a legal forfeiture whose curse alights on the body, and Calvin grants it as a mark of the curse while refusing to read it as a verdict on the man’s soul.
outliers: Clarke alone turns the verse into an argument against contemporary penal practice, condemning gibbeting on the ground that it never deterred the crimes it displayed.
